If the hon. member thinks it is not a good idea, perhaps it is because she is from the Ottawa area. The hon. member has the right to her own opinion, but I think a good decision has been made for the farmers and for agriculture in Canada.

Mr. Speaker, I appreciate the participation of the hon. minister in the debate and the brief outline of the government's positions on international trade.
He said that the Canadian tradition is reasonable. I was pleased to hear that because this morning we heard the view of the Minister of Grains and Oilseeds which was definitely anything but reasonable. He was not taking a position between the Americans and the Europeans as this minister describes the official government line to be. The Minister of Grains and Oilseeds was damning the Europeans outright and blaming all the trade war on the Europeans. He was ignoring the marketing facts, that 40 per cent of the grains market in the world is controlled by the United States. Only about 20 per cent, usually slightly less, is made up of sales from the dozen or more countries making up the European Economic Community and approximately the same by Canada.
The U.S. dominates the trade. They set the price.
If we are going to do anything about price, raining our damnation on the Europeans is not going to solve the problem. I hope that this minister will be a little more forthright at the cabinet table and make certain that some of the rest of his colleagues follow what he says is the government line once we get beyond the borders of this country.
When I hear him, it makes much more sense than when I listen to the minister for grains and oilseeds whose position makes no sense at all and defies reason.

speakerposition: Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs; Minister of State (Agriculture)
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would say to my hon. friend that we have been in that business for years and years. He knows very well that when I say that we are between the Europeans and the Americans, what I ment was that with the balanced position we have with the supply-management system where we ask to strengthen and clarify Article XI of GATT, we are put in the middle because we have some allies in Europe, in Asia and other areas. The Americans are very cold to the Canadian position. That is what I mean.

For the grain sector, I agree with the Minister of Grains and Oilseeds. Obviously, we have defended our position for years and years for the export subsidy war that we have. We all ask for those subsidies that destroyed our agriculture in the west to be put aside.
What I meant when I said that was that it put us in the middle. On the other side, the supply-management system is supported by the opposition and the whole agriculture community across the country. It put us in a more delicate situation and more in the middle. I do not want to be misunderstood.

Mr. Minister, in your answer yesterday regarding Canada's position on Article XI in the present GATT talks in Europe and our concerns in this respect, you said in concluding that until the government decided otherwise, it would defend Article XI. I would appreciate an answer from the Minister of State (Agriculture). Does this mean that despite any pressure from other parties, you still have a moral commitment to Canadian farmers to maintain this article which is extremely important for the agricultural industry? Do you have a moral commitment?

speakerposition: Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs; Minister of State (Agriculture)
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I appreciate the question put by the hon. member for Gatineau-La Lievre, and I would like to clarify Canada's position, because I know there are various rumours doing the rounds about Canada's position on Article XI. Mr. Speaker, Canada's position on Article XI is clear and has not changed one bit. We support Article XI. We want it to be clarified and reinforced, because its present wording, and everyone is agreed on this point, does not give us the kind of
flexibility we would like for our marketing board programs.
The problem, Mr. Speaker-and I think it is useful to repeat this, since it is an important point-the problem is that among those who support this position in Europe and elsewhere, some parties may be more reluctant to support us. However, although some people might have changed their minds, this does not mean that Canada has changed its mind. We have not changed our position. We have no intention of doing so, but we must be vigilant, and I am sure I can count on the hon. member's support. We must be extremely vigilant to ensure that we can maintain a strong position in the international community among 99 or 100 other countries, a position that will be and that continues to be to defend Article XI and to reinforce and clarify it. That is where we are now.
A week or two from now I will in Geneva, Mr. Speaker, to meet the Director General of GATT, and I will also be meeting the President of the Union des producteurs agricoles du Quebec very shortly, in Europe, to discuss this matter.

Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to join in this debate today which I think, without question, concerns a very, very important motion.
At the outset I think we should emphasize that this motion was passed in the Standing Committee on Agriculture in the last week in August. It was passed unanimously, which means that all members present and all parties supported this motion at that time. It disappoints me greatly that the Minister of Grains and Oilseeds this morning told this House and Canadians why today his party cannot support the motion. It makes it very clear that in the motion and in the statement following the motion, it would not be considered by anyone as a vote of non-confidence in the government. I think we should make it very clear that the government members said on August 28 or 29-1 forget the date- they support the motion, but today they are indicating that when they vote on it next Monday night-I believe it is going to be a deferred vote-they are not going to support it. I think that begs the question of Conservatives, did they mean what they said at the standing committee or not?
September 19, 1991

Anyway, on with the topic. What we are talking about here, Mr. Speaker, is a very, very important industry. It is a wealth-creating industry in this country, and there are only four of them: fishing, farming, forestry and mining. Everything that we have, as I said before in this House, before us and used as Canadians comes from one of those basic natural resources. We go on with farming and with all of them. We provide for the needs of ourselves and our society from that. We have an industry here that is in bad trouble, a bad financial situation.
There are 425,000 to 450,000 Canadians involved in the industry. There are many total communities that are involved in that industry. At the present time, we have a tremendous amount of disappointment in the government and what it has said in the last two or three years and what has happened. The minister who just spoke said that the plans and the support programs that have been put in place for the future were done in conjunction with and with the assistance of the farming community, and indeed farmers themselves and their organizations. I agree, that did take place, Mr. Speaker. But when those groups were asked to come forward and take part in planning their future and come up with the right ideas, they were told and they were led and they were shown very clearly by the government that in the transition from our old ad hoc type assistance programs to agriculture to a new safety net program, that in that transitional period they would not be let down.
However, that let-down has happened. Producers in this country, primary producers in the agricultural industry, are asking the government to reconsider and to live up to that promise and that commitment, and that has not come forward.
That is why I am getting phone calls from farm suppliers. That is why I am getting phone calls from individuals, from farmers who say "Lyle, I took over my father's farm. My father had some savings and some equity in the business, but I cannot survive. My parents are putting more money into my business every year and now they are having everything they had disappear". In the meantime our food producing abilities in this country are going down the drain and closing up every day, day after day.
Supply
I just want to give the public some information to look at. Ontario soft winter wheat farmers this year got $75 a tonne for the wheat they delivered in August from this year's crop.
Last year I believe that was $115 per tonne or $120 per tonne. I asked how many people took that type of drop. If we just want to convert that to what the farmer gets out of that, in a 500-gram box of cereal which is said to be 100 per cent wheat, at $75 a tonne the farmer got less than 4q for the wheat that was in that box of cereal that probably sold for three dollars-plus in the grocery store.
In 1933, if we look at the figures, the price relative to what farmers are getting for their products compared to the cost of living and the cost of doing business today is as bad or worse than it was in the dirty thirties.
In 1933 it took about three bushels of wheat for a man to get a haircut. Today it takes five. I am using wheat, although I could use other crops, but that seems to be the one we use as a yardstick.
For an average retirement home in 1933 it took less than 7,000 bushels of wheat. If a farmer sold that, he could buy an average retirement home. In 1991, instead of less than 7,000 bushels of wheat, it will take 60,000 bushels of wheat. That is some comparison.
In 1933 the average man's dress shirt would take five bushels of wheat. You could sell that and go to town and buy a dress shirt. Today it takes 15 bushels of wheat. I could go on, but I think that brings home the point.
There is another matter. Farmers keep saying to me: "Lyle, we have concerns about the environment, but are we not a little bit out of whack? Where are we here?" We talk about sustainable agriculture and sustainable environment, et cetera. Yes, I agree with this sustainable environment and I promote it and I support it. But I maintain that unless an industry is sustainable economically, it cannot sustain the environment as well. If the industry is not there, so what?
I have farmers and individuals and other business people who have nothing to do with agriculture coming to me and saying: "Are we not a little out of whack?" In society today it takes between $150 to $200 to dump, or the term that is used is to "tip" a load of garbage. That is

Supply
on average what it takes to get rid of a load of garbage in today's society.
The Ontario fanner gets $75 for a tonne of wheat. As one chap said to me the other day, why do we not eat the garbage and dump the wheat? We cannot survive on that. Nobody can survive on that.
The other fact I want to mention is that the average farmer in Canada today feeds between 95 and 100 Canadians. That is their production. We are in an incredibly efficient, excellent industry. The average farmer feeds between 95 and 100 Canadians, while the farmers' spouses, be that the man or the lady in the house, goes out and finds work off the farm so that that farmer can afford to put groceries on the farm family's table. There is increasing difficulty in finding jobs out there in the rural communities, because we are losing jobs across this country.
We are now in a situation where the spouse cannot even go out and find that farm. As the minister of grains and oilseeds said this morning, the average farmer in Canada today has $6,300 left after they do their business in order to maintain their homes and in order to look after their families. We talked a lot about fairness this week. I do not think that is fair.
We are talking about interim GRIP payments coming forward. Yes, that money is going to be welcome, but it is not providing the transitional assistance for that one year gap until the GRIP and NISA gets up and running and does what we all hope it is going to do. There is a big let-down here.
What the government is saying is that it will make an interim GRIP payment this fall. That is the same as me saying to you that I know you are having difficulty making your November mortgage payments on your home this year, but I tell you what we will do, we will bring your next year's November cheque to you and you can have it this November to use. But just remember, there will not be a pay cheque next November.
So what we are doing and what the government is doing is saying that we are prepared to reach into next year, bring next year's income back to this year and hope that somebody looks after you next year.
I would just like to make one other statement before I sit down. We know there are a lot of farmers going out to
meetings. In Lucknow, Ontario last week there were over 1,000 fanners out. In Miami, Manitoba last week there were over 1,000 farmers out. But I think it is summed up by a statement, and I will quote, from a Mr. Bev Hill, who is quite well known and well respected and a very clever young chap in Ontario, and I will close with this. He stated this at a meeting last week in Ontario and I think it sums up the feeling of the total farm community: "Our fields of dreams have become acres of anguish".

Mr. Speaker, I would like to make a few comments. I too would like to participate in this debate, which I truly think is about the current plight of the farmers and what the government has for them in an emergency.
When we heard the minister telling us earlier that he would not take ad hoc measures, I wondered if the minister had understood the meaning of an emergency.
One imagines in a health setting that you know the diagnosis of the patient and then somehow something happens unpredictably and there is an emergency. You take an ad hoc measure. You take an emergency measure to avoid the imminence of death.
To the issue before us today, there is no doubt about the diagnosis. There is a crisis among our fanners. There is a shortfall of cash flow. The standing committee of this House on agriculture has made that ascertainment. So, there is no doubt about that. We, in fact, know the two fundamental causes.
First, because of the non-resolution of the international trade war. That, to me, is a failure of leadership on the part of this government for not being able to bring this forward to a speedy and complete resolution.
The second major cause is that this government has failed to have real, meaningful support programs for 1989 and 1990.
Just in my province of Manitoba, concerning the 1991 cash advance of over $300 million, I am advised that over $63 million is still outstanding, and you are asking the farmers to absorb the whole gross income decrease of 25 per cent in 1990 and a 30 per cent drop in 1991.
I would like to ask my colleague for his comments. What is the value of making a special grains payment at this time as an emergency to allow us a transition before
September 19, 1991

Supply
we allow the support programs to take their natural course of support. I would like to ask my colleague to please respond to that.

Mr. Speaker, I would be pleased to respond to that.
I think, without question, that requirement of that transitional payment is absolutely necessary. I recognize that during this time we are in a bad deficit situation as a country. Even in those situations there are emergencies, whether it is in our personal life or in our business. We are at a real crisis. I have farmed all my life and we are in a crisis such as we have never seen before.
The agriculture community went through a shakedown in the late 1970s and the early 1980s, part of which I went through. It was said then that we will shake it down. There will be some fall-out. The inefficient will fall out and what is left will be our efficient farmers and we will go on from there.
We are going through a worse shake-down than that. We are tearing families and homes apart. We as a House of Commons, as a Parliament and Canada as a country need now to make that decision. It is a very simple question. Is agriculture and food security, and I could go on and on, important to Canada or is it not? To me the answer to that is very simple. It definitely is, not only in the short term but in the long term. If we do not keep that industry and all the spin-offs through manufacturing et cetera that is involved with it, it will not be here for our children and our grandchildren.
This government and all governments like to talk about what we are going to do for our children and our grandchildren. I maintain, and I speak very strongly on this, this is one thing we had better do for those who follow us, maintain this industry.

Mr. Speaker, first of all, I would like to thank my colleague from Prince Edward- Hastings for sharing his time with me this afternoon.
I am happy that the House of Commons has set aside the time to address one of the most important issues facing our country, the farm financial crisis. The crisis is not exclusive to the prairie provinces or to Ontario and Quebec. It also includes the maritimes in most sectors in the industry. It is a national crisis. It affects farmers in the agri-food industry right across this whole country.
There is a great deal of uncertainty in the dairy industry, one of our most stable sectors, because of the GATT negotiations and the rumours that have been emanating from Geneva. I hope that the mandate given to our negotiators is an inflexible one. Article XI of GATT must be protected and extended. The retention of Article XI is paramount if we are to keep our supply managed commodities, which guarantee at least the cost of production for the farmers involved in these commodities.
I urge the government to hold fast to the position of retaining and strengthening Article XI. It would be a sad day for Canada if our dairy industry was reduced to the chaotic state that the American dairy industry is, where bankruptcy is a very common occurrence.
I want to address my main remarks to the unfolding tragedy of the potato industry in Prince Edward Island and New Brunswick and especially in Prince Edward Island where potatoes have been the cornerstone of our economy since the colonial days.
P.E.I. basically has two wealth-generating resources, agriculture and fisheries. The health of these two industries is vital to our whole economy. We have no mining in Prince Edward Island. We have no rivers large enough to harness hydroelectricity and no gas and oil deposits. Agriculture is the industry which is most vital to P.E.I. and our table and seed potato industry is the most important sector of that industry.
We have long enjoyed a world-wide reputation for our seed and table potatoes. Our seed is in demand in Europe and South America, in Africa and Mexico, the United States and the rest of Canada. Potatoes growing from P.E.I. seed out-produced seed from any other source in the world, including Holland, the next most important source of seed. The potato industry has been an industry which has competed in a world market for many years virtually on its own.
If you are looking for an example of an agricultural commodity which is operated in a free-market system, the capitalist, international, non-subsidized milieu, you will find it in P.E.I. seed and table potato industry. Rarely, and only in times of world over-production and two-cent a pound potatoes, have Prince Edward Island producers looked for government assistance in order to survive.

September 19, 1991
Supply
For the most part, the industry has competed head to head with the world with little extraordinary assistance from the Canadian taxpayer.
P.E.I., Canada's smallest province, competed against a nation, the Netherlands, in seed quality, and won.
The victory was not won overnight. It took years and the efforts of generation of farmers to achieve this position. It took support from Agriculture Canada over many years in developing new seed varieties, identifying new markets, inspection and protection services. It took many years of support from the provincial government which augmented and facilitated the efforts of the farm community and Agriculture Canada.
This combination of ideal soil and environmental conditions, with industrious, progressive farmers, who are committed to quality, disease-free stocks, in co-ordination with governments, has enabled the potato industry in Prince Edward Island to withstand the ups and downs of a very volatile industry. There were many poor years, and fewer good ones, but enough to sustain the industry over the long term.
But this scenario has been brought to an abrupt halt with the discovery of the potato virus Y-N strain in our potato crop. There is zero tolerance for this virus in North America. This discovery has closed the door to the exports of our potatoes to our largest markets, the United States and the rest of Canada.
Europe, which has had the disease for over 50 years, has established a tolerance level for the virus which has enabled the European community to live with the virus which they had to do because its elimination and eradication was impossible.
I must remind the House that the potato virus Y does not affect human beings in any way, shape or form.
All potatoes have the PVY virus of one strain or another. The problem with the potato virus Y-N strain is that it is deadly to tobacco. It destroys tobacco.
The transmission to the Americans of the information that P.E.I. had PVY-N resulted in the immediate closure of the American border to P.E.I. seed. The embargo was soon extended to include table stock unless sprayed with a sprout inhibitor. Canada, after protesting to Washington about how unfair this was, followed the American example and closed Canada's borders.
These actions, of course, brought the potato industry in Prince Edward Island into chaos.
The lack of time prohibits me from going into a step-by-step unfolding of the drama to this point in time. It is sufficient to say that an eradication compensation program was put into effect for the 1990 crop in an effort to contain and eliminate the disease. A massive leaf testing offensive was put in place for the 1991 crop. Millions of leaves were tested in P.E.I., but considerably less testing was done in other provinces.
Ninety-six new cases of PVY-N were discovered in Prince Edward Island, ten in Ontario and a few in the other provinces.
PVY-N was said to be found in varieties which were PVY-N-free last year. The eradication program for the 1990 crop seemed to have been a failure, that is until the validity of Agriculture Canada's testing methodology was brought into question.
Independent scientists have brought into question Agriculture Canada's methods and results which, if proven correct, means that there has been a misdiagnosis of the virus.
Agriculture Canada's 96 positive cases may not be PVY-N at all, but rather a fusion of other PVY strains which can produce the same result when swabbed on tobacco leaves.
As one commentator said, the Island was ploughed down for nothing and its main industry destroyed. This whole sad tale has produced a whole series of questions which have not and may never be answered.
(1)	If PVY-N was rampant on Prince Edward Island, why has there been no infection of the P.E.I. tobacco crop, no infection whatsoever? Our tobacco producers have absolutely no fear of infection saying that if there are PVY-N infected potatoes, a regular spray program will take care of the aphids.
(2)	Where did the PVY-N virus come from in the first place? How was it introduced to Prince Edward Island? One thing is sure, this government with its centralization program and taking scientists and virologists from the provinces to Ottawa only means that it will be easier to have diseased stock coming into this country in the future.
September 19, 1991

(3)	Why has the state of Maine been able to dictate to the USDA and Agriculture Canada on the lifting of the border restrictions? Maine has tried for years to prevent P.E.I. potatoes from entering the state or passing through the state. They have tried anti-dumping procedures and border harassment. You name it, they have tried it and have failed.
Maine was losing out badly to Prince Edward Island and New Brunswick seed and table producers, and indeed to table producers from the western U.S. states. They failed to keep up with advancements in the industry and their products could not compete.
As far as Maine is concerned, the PVY-N crisis is the best thing that has happened for them in years, and they do not mean to let go. They and Senator Mitchell are calling the shots on this one, and our government does not have the political or moral courage to take them on.
(4)	Are Agriculture Canada's testing procedures up to date and accurate? Other scientists think not and, if proven correct, this could be the crudest cut of all. It is possible that the whole problem has been blown vastly out of proportion and the reputation of P.E.I. potatoes and Agriculture Canada has been destroyed.
(5)	Why has the United States not tested for PVY-N? After all, if we have it, they have it because we have been shipping potatoes into the United States since the time we are told it was first discovered in P.E.I. in 1987. Therefore, they have PVY-N if we have it. As long as the United States does not test-they say they do not have it-is this really logical? If we both have it and it cannot be eradicated, why not strike a tolerance level?
(6)	Why has it taken so long to get the 1990 compensation cheques issued? Why are there no forms for the 1991 compensation claims?
Elow would you, Mr. Speaker, or any of us in this House like not to have been paid during the past year? These farmers are living on bank loans for over a year. This must be corrected.
To conclude, I want to make a few remarks about the farm financial crisis in general.
It is a fact that our farm debt is $24 billion. Interest on this debt at the rate of 10 per cent is $2.5 billion. That means the over $2 billion the government bragged it is going to put into the farm sector this year is merely going

to pay the interest on the farm debt. The only ones really getting paid are the bankers.
Mr. Speaker, thank you very much. I would like to say a few things more, but you have indicated that my time is up. Thank you.

Mr. Speaker, my colleague from Egmont and the speaker before him have demonstrated how productive farmers in general are. There is no doubt about that. In turn, our colleague from Prince Edward-Hastings described production, past and present. There is no doubt that they are indeed very productive.
I have a question for my colleague at this point. About the answers the Minister of Agriculture and the Minister of State (Agriculture) provided yesterday, the problem is that farmers or producers are requesting protection. We know that agriculture has become as important as national defence. There is no doubt about it, we cannot rely on production from abroad as regards agriculture. We must be self-sufficient. That is a steadfast rule. Here is my question. The Quebec UPA made several representations and, contrary to what I was told in both answers I received yesterday, they asked for our borders to be protected so as to prevent dumping. According to the UPA, the former Minister of Agriculture, the hon. Eugene Whelan was a man of great convictions. I was told that he was the father of joint programs. He is. However, what Canadian farmers need right now is protection.
So, I ask my colleague: is protection provided for in joint programs, is there a moral commitment on the part of the government or is it just left open in the free market? We suggest that government involvement is required to keep the market in line. However, would the government not endanger the Canadian farm industry by claiming that the best approach is to force farmers to produce beyond their capacity?

Mr. Speaker, one thing is certain. That is if Canada continues on its present road, it will not be self-sufficient in food, while at the same time the Americans have made it much easier for their farmers to become more productive and to shed their burden of debt.

September 19, 1991

For example, the Americans have set up a system which includes debt forgiveness and they have restructured their debt forgiveness procedures putting their farmers at a considerable advantage over ours. They have, over the long term, come to the conclusion that the debt load their farmers were carrying was just too heavy. They took the attitude that the situation in the United States was like an airplane flying at 30,000 feet which was absolutely certain to come down. The choice was whether it would have an easy glide and a fairly soft landing, or it would crash. These are the same options that our government has today. Is it going to make the landing a little softer, or is it going to let the agricultural community crash and be destroyed, thereby making Canada reliant for her food resources on other countries?
Mr. Speaker, I just wanted to take the opportunity to compliment the hon. member for Egmont, from my province, for his comments on this very serious issue.
Hear, hear.

I especially appreciated his comments on the PVY-N virus, the crisis we are having in our province at the present time.
I know my time is limited so I just want to mention one thing that the member referred to, and that is the compensation claims that the potato farmers have made for their 1990 crop. Four hundred compensation claims were sent to the government and at present only a hundred of our potato farmers have received any money. That seems like a long time to wait for the money, and certainly it is putting many farmers into very serious financial problems. I think it is very unfair for the government to expect farmers to wait this length of time and I would call on the government to do everything possible to speed up this process.

Mr. Speaker, I think it is worth while to review the resolution: "In view of the desperate financial cash flow crisis facing Canadian grains and oilseeds and horticultural producers the House of Commons calls on the Government of Canada to consider the advisability of providing cash assistance that would have been provided under the Gross Revenue Insurance Program and the Net Income Stabilization Account, had they been in place for 1990-91".
I read that resolution to remind members in the House, all 295 of us, that we are not instructing the government, that is the cabinet, but we are simply asking it to consider the advisability of helping at this time. That is why various members have expressed their disappointment that the Minister of Grains and Oilseeds chose to say that this was considered by the government as a matter of non-confidence. He said that the rules and the procedure in the House required it to be so. However, the Speaker at that time did not rule that way. The Speaker at that time, quoting from one of the books of authority-and I do not recall exactly which one-said that the government can decide whether a vote is or is not a vote of non-confidence. This leads me to believe that the minister at that time could have said: "We agree, it is not a vote of non-confidence, we agree that it is simply advising the cabinet of how the members in the House feel; that they think it is an emergency and that they think it is an emergency that can be helped by a cash infusion at this time and that we think it is proper that cash infusion be made at this time".
However, presumably the minister, on behalf of cabinet, did not want the members to be able to vote that way. What he was really doing when he said it would be considered a vote of non-confidence was reminding the members on the Tory side of the House that they would be required to vote against this resolution when it comes to a vote. He did not want them to have the right to vote for it because in committee they expressed that right by voting for this very same resolution. He did not want them to have that right in the House.
One can only wonder why. One can only hope that the government does have plans to make this kind of cash infusion. One can hope that it is going to use it for political purposes just as it did five years ago when it approved during an election campaign in Saskatchewan a cash infusion of one billion dollars under similar circumstances one week before the farmers went to the polls and voted, along with the other voters in Saskatchewan.
Let us hope that it has the same plan in mind this time and that some time during the election campaign, which is to be announced momentarily just as it is in B.C., the government will decide: "Yes, it is just and proper that we help the farmers not just in Saskatchewan but all over Canada at this time. So we have decided that we are going to make this kind of cash infusion". That it will happen one week before election day is perhaps fortuitous for the Tory government in Saskatchewan but even more important for the farmers, in particular the wheat producers, in that province. Farmers all over Canada are
September 19, 1991

suffering in the same way, and the resolution speaks of them as well.
The Minister of State for Agriculture toward the close of his remarks-he did not say it really-hinted that there was going to be an important announcement in Saskatchewan. When he was told that it had already been announced, then he said: "This is certainly going to please the farmers of Saskatchewan".
I am talking about the just announced move of Farm Credit Corporation to Regina. This is supposed to make the farmers happy. I do not know what it is going to cost to make that move. We have heard of other government agencies moving. Here is another one. Is it going to cost $5 million, $50 million, $100 million? We do not know at this time. We have not found out yet what it is going to cost in total to move the Energy Board to Calgary.
At a time of restraint, to put those millions of dollars, however many they are, into moving an office, when that money could be used to good effect to help the producers seems to me to be a poor example of restraint.
It was suggested by my colleague, the hon. member for Mackenzie, that perhaps the reason that Farm Credit is moving to Regina is because it would be much more efficient for them to deal with the foreclosures of farm properties in Saskatchewan if they are right there on the scene. One wonders just why at this particular time have they decided to spend money on that kind of a program as opposed to doing something productive and proper to help the farmers in Canada at this very bad time.
A farmer's life anywhere in Canada is not a happy one. I think I am paraphrasing a line from Gilbert and Sullivan when I say that. There was discussion earlier today about marketing boards and about supply management.
The supply management farmers generally have it easier than the others, but even they do not have it easy. They do not know what they are going to get for their product, but they have some control over the selling price to the producer as opposed to the example given by the member for Prince Edward-Hastings. He said that a $3 box of cereal might return four cents to the producer.
Supply
There is one interesting thing about that that he did not mention. That is that everyone other than the producer gets a fair return for his or her labour. The only one who does not get anything near the cost of producing that grain is the producer. Everyone else gets it because they have a guaranteed mark-up. Right up until the time that the consumer purchases that box of cereal, everyone gets a mark-up, everyone other than the producer because the producer has no control over his or her price. Everyone else has that control.
With supply managed products the producers generally have enough control that they do get the cost of production out of it. It is the one area in agriculture where consumers are paying what it costs to produce the product. In every other area of agriculture the producers do not always get the return equal to the cost of production or anything near it.
Certainly that applies to the grain growers, it applies to fruit growers, it applies to horticultural crops generally where there is not this protection that is afforded to those farmers who are able to engage in supply management.
Even with supply management, farmers cannot be sure of getting a decent return. They are fighting the elements. It is said that Canadians have a higher per average cost of energy than people in any other industrialized nation in the world. We do live further north. It does cost more for energy. We need more energy in almost everything we are doing.
The Minister of State for Agriculture talked about the efficiency of Canadian producers and that is true. They are very efficient. We are very efficient.
Mr. Speaker, I know my time is about up, and I will just say this. Of all the people in the community who cannot have any control over the selling price, the producers are the ones that at the present time need this cash infusion. The government is abandoning its responsibility to a large section of the community when it says that its own members will not have the right to simply advise cabinet at this time. This responsibility should be recognized by letting the members vote and give the cabinet this kind of advice.

That would eliminate the surprise and political advantage if it were announced here and now. or $2 billion program to help the farmers. For partisan political reasons the government is instructing its own members to vote against this resolution today so the cabinet can make it public some three or four weeks from today.

In fact, it was his response to a question I had placed before him about farm finance.

I would like to ask the member, who was a minister in British Columbia, how the move of the head office and some employees to Regina at the cost of a few million dollars is going to make farmers happy and make them feel more comfortable with their financial situation and the fact that there is not going to be another dime put in their pockets. How does he think the farmers will react to moving the head office of FCC to Regina?

Mr. Speaker, I can only anticipate that the farmers will be very disappointed when they hear about the resolution that has been debated and is still being debated in this House today, when they see us vote on it and the government members defeat it.
I am very disappointed that the government feels proud about spending another x millions of dollars to move an office from one part of the country to another when it could have been spending that money in announcing a program to help the farmers who are desperate for that kind of assistance. I expect they will be disappointed. I hope they will react properly when they get the opportunity to vote.

Madam Speaker, it is a pleasure to rise today and speak in favour of this motion which is asking for a third line of defence cash assistance on an emergency basis to
September 19, 1991

provide certain levels of support to the farmers who are facing crisis in Canada.
Although the concentration so far has been on grains and oilseeds, the resolution also refers to other horticultural producers. It is some of those other horticultural producers that I hope to speak about and bring to the House's attention. Although in Canada we have a concentration on the bread basket of Canada, being the prairie provinces, and our grains and oilseeds area, a very important sector of our community, we often have a tendency to forget that there are other pockets of agriculture and horticulture throughout Canada, areas such as the Okanagan, Similkameen, the Nicola Valley and Merritt area and the boundary country of which I am the representative. There are also areas in the Niagara Peninsula and Annapolis, fruit-growing areas of this country and the cattle areas of this country.
We know that the producers of grain on the prairies are hurting. This is in response to that. However, I am here to tell this House and the people of Canada that people in my area, the grape growers, the fruit growers, cattlemen and women, farmers of all stripes and descriptions are hurting. They are looking for help and guidance. They are tired of the bankrupt ideas of this government and governments of similar ilk who continue to tell them not only to make it on their own but continue to turn their backs on them in their time of need.
In my area we have just come through the second summer after the free trade agreement and have seen some of the problems it has created. It may perhaps be only a perceptual problem but a problem nevertheless. Last summer, for instance, the cherry growers in my area witnessed a massive dumping of product from the United States into Canada at well below production cost not only in Canada, but well below the production cost in the state of Washington. Although there was not that much of a benefit to the Washington growers, they perceived that because of the free trade agreement they had a new and open market. They gave benefits to their purchasers that the growers in Canada could not touch.
We witnessed toward the end of last summer and throughout the fall and winter acres of cherry trees being ripped out. This was just directly after, in my area, watching approximately 2,000 acres of vineyards being
Supply
ripped out as a result of the free trade agreement and GATT rulings.
Over the past year I personally have watched some young farmers, up and coming, advanced, enthusiastic farmers, losing their enthusiasm for the land. There is not a farmer out there who can make it on agriculture alone. Either he, she or the spouse has to go and find another job in order to try to make a little extra money to keep their families and pay for their mortgage. When you are a farmer, it becomes a labour of love as opposed to a way of making a living.
I have watched these young farmers not only lose their interest in the land but turning their backs on the land, letting the banks take it back or trying to sell it. That becomes a very great problem also, because right now it is often difficult to sell 10, 15 or 20 acres of orchard land because everybody knows you cannot make a living as a fruit farmer.
There are things this government must do. We must face up to the reality that we want to continue to be able to produce food in Canada. Most Canadians want to ensure that we have a viable agriculture industry. We have to look at short-term benefits for these farmers as set out in this motion, not just to the grain farmers, but to other farmers in Canada, the fruit farmers, the grape growers and the cattlemen.
Lately in the fruit farming area they have run into low prices. They have run into the usual things farmers can expect, inclement weather, massive destruction as a result of hail; low crops in some cases because of a late spring and a freeze-out of various crops or a very cold winter during which a number of farmers lost trees.
The farmer is told to get up to date on what is being sold. In British Columbia they were offered $3,000 for each acre of replant, but it costs anywhere up to $11,000 or $12,000 an acre and they are told by the banks that they are not good risks. Well, where do they come up with the money to improve their lot, to ensure that they have a product that meets the needs of the market?
I spoke recently to a farmer from Oliver, B.C., and he told me how he has over the last little while diversified into a number of different apple crops in order to get a higher price. But the cost of that is enormous.

Supply
The Minister of State for Agriculture has talked to us about competitiveness, yet these farmers run into problems with the high cost of borrowing and the high cost of storage. In order to get a higher price for their product they have to have conditioned atmosphere storage, the cost of which is enormous. Again, they have to borrow money. With the various problems in marketing, they are having difficulty repaying some of these loans.
Whether we look at it in the short term or the long term, the agricultural industry in Canada is in major difficulty. They need a hand this year to assist them to pull themselves up by the boot straps so they can live to fight another day. Just as important, they need a government that is feeling and sensitive to what is required in the long term.
In our area it is education. The farmers need assistance in running their farms as a business. They need education in new and upgraded methods of agriculture. They need the time and ability to get that education. They need the assistance in investigating new markets. Although they have to be expected, to some extent, to find some of those markets, they have to be given proper assistance and show of support by this government to find those markets.
I cannot emphasize enough how important this particular motion is to the farmer, because of its over-all look at agriculture and the long-term needs of this country.

speakerposition: Deputy House Leader of the Official Opposition; Liberal Party Deputy House Leader
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I welcome this opportunity to take part in today's debate on a motion asking the government to assist the Canadian agricultural industry. This afternoon,
I would like to raise a few points in connection with grain production and subsequently, I intend to discuss the present and future status of GATT talks. Finally, Madam Speaker, I think I should tell the House about some rather depressing events in the agricultural sector in Glengarry-Prescott-Russell.
Madam Speaker, this has been a difficult year for Ontario grain producers. For instance, the price of com, soy beans and wheat is 35 per cent below what it was last year and 45 per cent less than the 15-year average. If the prices of these commodities remain uncharged, Madam Speaker, Ontario farmers alone will suffer a $175 million shortfall this year, compared to last year.

I have before me a chart. It compares the cost of com flakes with the price of corn. In 1980, corn sold for 15 cents a kilogram. Corn flakes sold for $2.21 a kilogram. In 1990, corn sold for 14 cents a kilogram, less than 1980 by 1 cent. Guess what happened to the price of com flakes. It jumped from $2.21 to $4.28. In other words, while the price of this particular product to farmers was decreasing, the price to the consumer doubled.
Canadians have reason to complain about the prices, but it is not the farmers who are getting the money. Of course, notwithstanding the fact that some of those middle people are getting more than their fair share, we still manage to have the second lowest food prices as a proportion to our income of any nation on earth.

On August 29 this year, the hon. member for Algoma moved a motion at an emergency meeting of the Standing Committee on Agriculture of this House. In his motion, the hon. member asked the government to provide emergency assistance to grain producers, starting this year, because there would a gap between existing programs, or rather programs that existed until quite recently, and the new programs that will be introduced next year.
We need an emergency program during the transition period. As I said earlier, the hon. member for Algoma moved a motion asking the government to take this kind of action, and of course, the committee adopted the motion unanimously. And I congratulate members on all sides of this House, the Conservatives, members of our party, and all the others who voted, asking for government action. So far, however, no answers have been forthcoming.

We have a few more problems on the horizon.
Canadian farmers are veiy worried about what the Government of Canada intends to do at the GATT negotiating table. As you know, we are presently in the so-called Uruguay Round of the GATT negotiations. In this round, there is tremendous concern, and rightfully so, about the price of agricultural commodities, prices which have been deflated as a result of the subsidy war
September 19, 1991

between countries, more particularly the EEC nations and the United States.
Canada has been the victim of this. Canadian farmers are afraid, and I think they have every reason to be concerned, about the future of Article XI of the GATT agreement. Article XI presently permits supply management in agriculture. In simple language, it permits farmers to have quota systems where they wish to have them as producer organizations.
The negotiating team right now before the GATT is having discussions. That team was brought before the Standing Committee on Agriculture yesterday. Members of Parliament tried desperately to obtain assurances from our negotiating team that we had not offered to sacrifice Article XI of the GATT in exchange for something else.
Despite the best efforts of all MPs from all political parties, no such assurance came forward yesterday. I can tell you that I am very concerned. Usually when someone refuses to tell you something, there is a good reason for it, and I am very afraid about the future of Article XI.
Two members yesterday, the member for Haldimand- Norfolk and the member for Gatineau-La Lievre both asked in this House for the assurances of the government that Article XI of the GATT would be protected and strengthened. Do you know the answer they received? The Minister of State for Agriculture said, roughly, as follows: "There will not be any changes until we announce that there are changes." Well, that is a great reassurance for the dairy farmers of Canada.
The government has to announce clear policies, and has to assure the farmers that Article XI will continue and will be enhanced and not be done away with.

Madam Speaker, finally I would like to raise in this House a tragedy that happened in my riding about an hour ago. A reporter told me that a slaughterhouse in my riding, Viandes Saint-Isidore Inc. of St. Isidore de Prescott, Ontario, was closing down tomorrow, resulting in the loss of 40 jobs.
This company slaughtered about 5,500 pigs a week, Madam Speaker. At the end of the day today, while we
Supply
are making speeches in this House, slaughtering operations will cease in St. Isidore. Tomorrow evening, the factory will shut down completely. Of course, in my riding, with such a high unemployment rate, this bad news will be very hard for us to take.
In this case for once, at any rate, it does not seem to be due to free trade or something like that, but other government policies influenced the outcome, such as the policy of too high interest rates that hurt this company. Of course, there were other problems along the way.
But, Madam Speaker, it would be important to point out the price of farm products again. As I did earlier with corn, I will compare the price of bacon. Once again, I have here in front of me a diagram that compares prices in 1980 and 1988. In 1980, bacon sold for $1.30 a kilo-that is the price the farmer received. In 1990, he got $1.38 and today, as we speak, the price is about the same, $1.38 a kilo. The consumer, however, paid about $5.54 a kilo in 1980 and now pays about eight dollars. So in 1980, the consumer paid about four times what the farmer got. Today, it is more than six times. We need help for agriculture, Madam Speaker. I hope that the government will listen to the needs and for once try to help Canadian farming.

Madam Speaker, I congratulate my colleague once again on addressing the issue with specifics. I want to ask him a very specific question. One of the problems of those of us who spend most of our time in urban markets is our lack of information on the specific reasons why we have a farm crisis in this country. Many times today we have referred to the problems being caused by the European Common Market approach to agriculture and the tremendous subsidies.
Does the hon. member not think that as part of our strategy to win support for correcting this problem in the long term might be to develop a communications plan explaining this problem that is happening in rural Canada, in agriculture in Canada, which goes beyond that community itself? In other words, we go into the major markets not only here but also in Europe and explain exactly how these subsidies are putting our young farmers and our experienced farmers out of business.

Supply
Maybe through that kind of process we might get a more rational approach to the subsidy program that is being handled all over the world. I wonder if the hon. member could speak to that.

speakerposition: Deputy House Leader of the Official Opposition; Liberal Party Deputy House Leader
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I thank my colleague for his question. My colleague comes from an urban riding. One thing that I appreciate particularly is the fact that he as an urban member is always here when we are discussing agriculture. Whereas I cannot speak of the presence or absence of any member singularly, I must tell you, Madam Speaker, how pleased I am when members who are from urban areas take that kind of an interest. That is the first step and I congratulate him for it. I wish all members had that same kind of interest.
Our colleague, the hon. member for Lambton- Middlesex, produced very good documentation about how in fact farmers are not getting their share of the revenues of agriculture. I for one will be putting out a householder to my constituents shortly to explain just the discrepancy, just like I described for the price of com and the price of hogs how the discrepancy between what the farmer is getting versus what the consumer has to pay and how it is progressively getting worse. We must continue to say that to all Canadians so that they understand.
We must do it not only in our agricultural constituencies. All MPs should do this across Canada. As well I think it is the duty of our government to try to make other nations understand what it is that we are doing. Effectively what we are doing is we are whipping each other with our dollars. That is what we are doing. We are completely inundating the situation with subsidies.
Farmers in other countries, particularly the United States and the EEC, are receiving huge subsidies. Those subsidies of course benefit nations which then purchase those commodities. It is unusual to see, for instance, that countries, what we used to refer to as eastern bloc countries, are buying food that was subsidized by the countries of the west because they are arguing with each other as to who should have the so-called rightful share of the market.

Madam Speaker, I just want to remind the member that in his comments about Article XI and our Canadian position at the GATT talks, the
minister, if he would recall, was very adamant yesterday on the position of the Canadian government and our position there. I would just like to read part of that answer of yesterday.
The Government of Canada has stated, as my colleagues have, its position on Article XI. We are not talking about weakening Article XI. What we have asked for, and what the policies of this government is, is that Article XI should be further clarified and strengthened. That has not been changed -
That is the position of the Canadian government. I would not want the message to go out from this House of Commons that that has been changed. We do support it. We have been consistent. This has been developed with the producers in consultation with the stakeholders of that industry and with the government as to how that position was developed, and that position has not changed.

speakerposition: Deputy House Leader of the Official Opposition; Liberal Party Deputy House Leader
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I will only read the following sentence. It goes like this:
That has not changed and will not change until the government says it will change.
That is the assurance that the minister gave yesterday, and it is not good enough.

Madam Speaker, the last few words of my friend here relate to one of the questions I wanted to ask the Minister of Agriculture. Yesterday, I and my colleague from Ontario asked for assurances from the Department of Agriculture that the government is committed to preserving quotas and defending, strengthening and clarifying Article XI of GATT which deals with quotas which impede the free market, etc.
Madam Speaker, if you look at the history of agriculture in Quebec, it is the whole history of Quebec you are looking at. In 1950-and this is not very far back, I am quite sure that most members here recall those years- there were 240,000 farmers in Quebec. Some 40 odd years later only about 45,000 are left. It is true that the average productivity has increased tremendously, much more than it was thought possible 40 years ago, nevertheless, agriculture remains one of the extremely important elements of a nation. No nation wants to depend on another for its daily bread. All want to be sure that their agriculture is in good health. One has only to look at the Common Market, where there is a real agricultural war,
September 19, 1991

if I can use that expression, where all the members want to protect their farm production.
Here in Canada, we created, under the previous government, a system of quotas for milk, pork or other commodities like grain. This is extremely important for our farmers and for the farmers of Quebec. We had a system which was more rational, where the government could intervene not to control the market but rather to discipline it, make it more human, if I can use that expression. There are three elements, for when you talk to farm producers, and I veiy often had discussion with them on this question, they say that there are three fundamental principles. The first, according to them, is that you must always have the guarantee that borders can be controlled, that is to say that you can prevent dumping on your own market. You know that all sorts of explanations are used, like globalization, etc., but you would be surprised to learn that, when they use the term "globalization", other countries make nice sentences, speak of productivity, and so on. All countries, of course, have ways to protect their own market. One must not be fooled by these words, but look at the reality.
There is one more thing that must be protected in the farming industry, it is the fact that Canadian producers- and I know the situation of farmers in Quebec-have always wanted a form of protection which I always considered as totally realistic and that is to guarantee their production cost. That has always been, if you will, their basic argument.
If a farmer could be sure from the beginning to recoup his production costs, he could survive, and someone would take over after him. That argument is familiar to all of us, except that, to this day, our neighbours in the South have never really applied the program of quotas.
I heard on the news that milk producers from the State of Vermont, will meet in the coming weeks. They even made known their intention to carry out some form of strike because Vermont farmers, mostly milk producers, have benefitted from a quota system similar to the one we have in Canada. Obviously, Madam Speaker, I wish them great luck. It will be a start. They will make Americans aware that a quota system which guarantees production cost recovery is undoubtedly a sensible thing.

But that is where a moral commitment is needed with all this argumentation by the government, with the answers that the Minister of Agriculture gave us when he said: "As long as the government does not decide otherwise, we will keep protecting Article XI of the GATT." But during the consultations known as "Growing together", a leader from the Union des producteurs agricoles pointed out to me that they had been consulted on that issue. We surely want a growing agriculture, not only in Quebec, but throughout Canada. But they said that they never felt that their production costs were guaranteed. And I think that we should address that issue. Farmers do not have that guarantee. We hear about productivity almost every day. But if farmers are not sure of getting back their production costs, if they are subject to the law of the jungle, as it is the case in the United States-When you consider that over 100,000 farms have been lost in the last few years in the States, you get an idea of how the big multinationals came into the agricultural world. They are literally quashing the family farm in the United States. However, here in Canada, we have a different way of seeing things.
We would like to have a guarantee, a moral commitment from the government, that we will not expose our farmers to the law of the jungle. We would like to offer them the support that is vital for the survival of agriculture, and that is what we would do by ensuring them the production cost. If it is impossible to give them such a commitment, that in my view is a moral one, what future can they hope for in farming?
That is basically the question we are asking in this House. If the Minister of Agriculture, his Quebec counterpart and the Minister of State for Agriculture would provide an answer, I am sure farmers throughout Canada, and especially in Quebec, would be very happy to have it.
But the two answers we got yesterday are not enough. We want support for our farmers, not just for today, but for the future, especially to assist the next generation.
Madam Speaker, I will ask again the Minister of Agriculture and his colleague, the Minister of State, to make a moral commitment to really support our farmers,

Madam Speaker, I would just like to thank all parties for allowing unanimous consent for me to carry on. Surely that, if nothing else, is a good example to the Canadian public who is watching that this place can work and we can work together effectively.
I would just like to put on record some of the Reform Party's policies regarding agriculture because I heard some comments in statements this afternoon and also in Question Period by the member for Portage-Interlake and also the Minister for Grains and Oilseeds reflecting the fact that I should perhaps answer the questions in Question Period on behalf of the Reform Party.
There are policies, facts and global things that are happening that we simply cannot deny. What we need to do is be very frank and honest in admitting that some
things are happening around the world that we need to be very clear on and realize that they are happening.
First, I would say that there is an increasing need, both internationally and domestically, to reduce rather than increase government subsidization of agriculture due to the inability of governments and the community at large to finance such subsidization in the long run.
Whether we like it or not, because of our national debt and the way things are going around the world, this is the way things are happening. We have to agree that whether we like it or not, that is what is happening.
The Reform Party recognizes that there is a need for transitional support to protect agricultural producers against policies over which they have no control, including international subsidies that increase supplies and depress prices. We have certainly seen that with the price of wheat and barley in this latest crop year.
We recognize that we cannot just completely eliminate subsidies, that simply cannot and will not happen. We need to provide transitional support.
As well, the member for Portage-Interlake made some comments quoting the Reform Party, leaving out some very important words. I will just quickly go over those.
The Reform Party believes that the agricultural producers should offer the rest of the world and the rest of the country a deal leading to a step-by-step reduction of government agricultural support, at home and abroad. Yes, we need to be leaders in this. Yes, I believe the agricultural sector is willing to make that step and become a leader in a step-by-step reduction if other economic sectors and our trading partners will do the same. That is where the hon. member left off his sentence half way through.
I believe the agricultural sector is willing to do that if, and only if, every other sector will do it at the same time. Then we would see an equality of sacrifice right across the country.
Looking internationally again, the Reform Party supports a trade distortion adjustment program to compensate for the adverse effects of subsidies by other countries. If we were looking at a ratio, for roughly every $5,000 that Canadians are subsidized in our agricultural industiy, the figure is approximately $10,000 for Ameri-

cans and $25,000 for Europeans. We ask: "How could those figures balance out?"
We need to see a government that is very aggressive dealing with Article XI that is firm at the GATT negotiations. We are looking to this government to be very tough, as the hon. member mentioned earlier, to go to the GATT and say: "We simply will not give up these things, we will be tough and we will continue to press for lowering subsidies around the world".
The Reform Party supports an agricultural policy based on market mechanisms with the objective of meeting the needs of consumers for safe, affordable and secure supplies of food.
"Where circumstances allow" is another phrase that my friend from Portage-Interlake left out. That would mean a shift from a government supported agricultural industry to an industry shaped by the free operation of comparative advantage between regions and commodities, free entry into all sectors of production and marketing and free trade on a global basis.
If any opposition party is opposed to free trade, that is its political prerogative. With the global economy becoming so small, we realize that with trade travelling so quickly, with communications travelling so quickly we are looking at a global market whether we like it or not.
Again, my friend mentioned this afternoon that the Reform Party is going to absolutely reduce and eliminate all subsidies whatsoever. He left off the first part of that sentence which was "if other domestic sectors and countries will do the same". Now, we are looking at an "if then" clause grammatically. If this happens at the national and at the international level then of course the Reform Party supports the phased reduction and elimination of all subsidies, support programs and trade restrictions.
This is what farmers are concerned about. These are what farmers in Beaver River are talking about. These are what farmers who in fact developed the Reform Party agricultural policy are concerned about.
When I look at what is happening in the agricultural sector, and at what is happening in my riding of Beaver River, which is very much agriculture intensive, people are saying they do not want handouts all the time, but that they are facing a very difficult time right now with
