That, in the opinion of this House, the government promote a summit level meeting at the United Nations on global security, to examine ways of implementing and strengthening the United Nations peacekeeping and enforcement mechanisms.
He said: Madam Speaker, it is timely that this motion has been drawn for debate today, timely because it affords us with an opportunity to sustain the momentum that has been building in the aftermath of the gulf conflict, in favour of strengthening the United Nations.
It is also timely in light of today's call for a UN force to intervene in the conflict in Yugoslavia. I think also of events in the Soviet Union, peace efforts in the western Sahara, Cambodia and Angola and the simmering situation in Iraq and the threats of further violence.
The motion that I present for the House today reads, as you have said:
That, in the opinion of this House, the government promote a summit level meeting at the United Nations on global security, to examine ways of implementing and strengthening the United Nations peacekeeping and enforcement mechanisms.
Here, in this motion, we are presented with an opportunity, a golden one at that, to encourage the building up of a mechanism that can allow the United Nations to fulfil its intended role.
We Canadians have a responsibility to use our prestige and expertise in the area of peacekeeping. We can use our reputation as a devoted member of the United Nations family to ensure that this historic opportunity is not lost. It is a responsibility that Canada and other governments should seize. Canada's participation in the gulf was done, as we recall, in the name of the United Nations. And when it was argued that the operations against Iraq did not follow the UN charter to the letter, the reply was that the UN security mechanisms were not in place. It was, therefore, impossible to expect to the UN Security Council to have full command and control of the enforcement of its resolutions.
September 19, 1991

Has the lesson been learned? The answer, as we stand today, months later, has to be no. The UN is today being called on to perform peacemaking duties in the tragic conflict in Yugoslavia and, once again, the excuse back to the European community and to others is that the UN is not prepared. This has a hollow sound to it and it puts at risk the credibility of the union to maintain security and peace.
It is important to follow up the criticisms of the gulf action with constructive action. Clearly our world needs a functioning UN security mechanism. It is a responsibility not only of governments but of individual parliamentarians to seize this moment to help build a reliable collective security system of enforceable international law. If we do not rise to this challenge, succeeding generations may well scorn us for having missed so great an opportunity to bring about an international system of law that can reliably prevent aggression.
Bernard Wood, the chief executive officer of the Canadian Institute for International Peace and Security, has offered this warning to Canada: "There will be another test before very long and probably it will come in some region that is not as much of an economic or strategic interest to major world powers. If at that stage this international consensus and the international security structure fail to respond with equal vigour and even-handedness, the cynics will then have been vindicated and more importantly, the world will have been plunged backward".
Canada should not allow this to happen. We have invested too much in working toward the dream of a strong and effective United Nations to allow this moment to pass without undertaking a major effort to build up security mechanism of the UN. We are investing too much of our resources, talents and hopes, whether it be in Central America, in the Middle East, in Cyprus, in Angola or elsewhere not to act now, now that there is a genuine openness about reforming and renewing the United Nations.
There are no lack of ideas for strengthening the United Nations in the aftermath of the gulf war. New and old proposals are finding a renewed interest. A mechanism for preventive peacekeeping is being promoted, for example, whereby as a deterrent to aggression, UN troops could be deployed along the border of any nation that is being attacked. Others are beginning to look seriously at implementing the provisions of Article 43 and 47 of the UN Charter. That would enable the UN to mount its own force rather than having to rely on a major power.
Private Members' Business
There are still other discussions of an early warning capacity for the UN to ensure that developing conflicts can be detected and prevented from escalating. The question is: how do we turn these ideas that have been thought through, plans have been laid, how do we turn them into political realities? Surely, that is a job for politicians and political leadership. The tired pace of diplomatic discussions in the cavernous committee rooms of the UN will not bring the UN into the 21st century. What is needed is an infusion of political will.
We recall that in the 1960s people spoke of a rising tide of expectation. That was in relationship to development and decolonialization. We need today a rising tide of expectations that the international institutions that we have will be strengthened. What is urgently required is an infusion of vision, innovation and a renewed commitment to the ideals of the UN Charter. The spirit of San Francisco, that lofty idealism of the founders of the United Nations, that was of course one of the first casualties of the cold war, must be rekindled. To relaunch that spirit, we need to focus high level political attention.
That is why I have proposed in this motion that the Canadian government promote the convening of a high level meeting on global security. Earlier this year, under the auspices of parliamentarians global action, legislators from Latin America, Europe, Asia and Africa gathered here in the House of Commons to discuss this issue. We were briefed by UN officials, we had members from all major parties and across party lines from abroad and the focus of our discussion and time together was UN collective security. We were looking at it in the perspective of the aftermath of the gulf conflict.
Two days later, after these briefings, we agreed on the Ottawa declaration on UN collective security. The key recommendation of our time together in that representative meeting is a call for a special session of the UN General Assembly on International Peace and Security. The need for such a high level meeting has been recognized not just by our group and by parliamentarians, but by eminent persons here in Canada and abroad. The World Federation of the United Nations Associations, headed by Canadian Maurice Strong, has called for a major conference on the UN in 1995, the 50th anniversary of the UN. On April 22, 32 leading spokespersons, statesmen, including Maurice Strong, Stephen Lewis, Sonny Ramphal, Edward Heath, Jimmy Carter, Robert MacNamara, Sir Brian Urquhart and Eduard Shevardnadze, called for a world summit on global governments. At their July summit meeting in London,

Private Members' Business
Prime Minister Mulroney and the leaders of the G-7 industrialized nations devoted unprecedented attention to the question of strengthening the UN security role. Listen for a moment to the G-7 political declaration. Here is what the G-7 leaders, including our Prime Minister, said:
We believe the conditions now exist for the United Nations to fulfil completely the promise of its founders. A revitalized United Nations will have a central role in strengthening the international order. The UN's role in peacekeeping should be reinforced and we are prepared to support this strongly.
A month earlier, in Berlin, our Prime Minister echoed the sentiment that no step could be more important in strengthening the international order than strengthening the UN itself. He said Canada would like to see the UN's capacity to prevent war enhanced. We would like to see the role of the Secretary General enhanced and the organization's peacekeeping capacity increased.
There is then, clearly, a great deal of enthusiasm. The groundwork has been put in place for political work, for the generating of political will.
Here we have the world leaders looking at how to strengthen the UN. What is needed today is for Canada and supportive governments to organize ourselves, to formally present a proposal at the current session of the United Nations General Assembly. That session opened earlier this week in New York, welcoming as we saw with world attention the Baltic nations, South Korea and others. There is a good chance that Canadian leadership will be supported and we can be instruments in the process of change.
But, in politics, as all of us in this House know, timing is everything, timing is crucial, and we must act now while there is still momentum behind strengthening the United Nations. For I fear that in a year or two that this present window of opportunity will have slammed shut.
And, what might this summit level meeting focus on, the summit level meeting that the motion encourages Canada to work for? Well, global security is, of course, a multifaceted concept and the issues of environment, development, disarmament and human rights are all key.
But I think there can be a broad agreement on a starting point. The issue of strengthening the UN's peacekeeping and other security mechanisms has been sorely neglected and I believe the circumstances are particularly auspicious to remedy this problem at this time. I believe that the establishment of an effective UN security system is, in many ways, the key to many of the other problems we face, providing a reliable alternative to the bloated military budgets that nations rely upon for their security.
Here is the challenge. A mechanism of collective security is the precondition for an extensive disarmament to take place. Governments, like citizens of any community, need to be able to call 911, they need to be able to summon an international fighting force or police force. This security mechanism, in turn, would free vast resources that are needed to meet the host of domestic and international problems of environment, of education, of health care. And so I am urging the Government of Canada to seize this opportunity to develop, in concert with others, the idea of preventive peacekeeping. This could have deterred Iraq from aggression. It could avoid future bloody conflicts. The UN should have this capacity. We cannot expect the United States of America to be the world's policeman. This is unacceptable to Canadians, unacceptable to the world community, as well as to many Americans.
Ironically there has never been a high level political meeting, never been high level political attention devoted to the question of strengthening peacekeeping and international security.
If we think back for a moment, there have been special sessions of the General Assembly devoted to disarmament. There have been a number of sessions devoted to development. We are now in the midst of preparing for a second major conference on the world's environment to be hosted in Rio de Janeiro, Brazil.
But there are no such plans to devote this kind of attention to the issue of how we strengthen the security role of the United Nations and so strengthen the sense of security and confidence of the nations of the world. This is in spite of the fact that the maintenance of peace
September 19, 1991

was intended to be the primary function of the United Nations. This was its raison d'etre.
Such an initiative would give the entire international community an opportunity to shape the new world order of which both President Gorbachev and President Bush have spoken. There is a good deal of healthy scepticism of this concept. The concern is that the new world order will be dictated by a single power.
By launching a global intergovernmental conference, all nations will participate in the shaping of this order. They can insist that it meet their immediate needs and the needs of the global community.
As a result of the Ottawa workshop of parliamentarians sponsored by Parliamentarians for Global Action and CUPS and other agencies here, that several of us who are here in the House tonight attended, there is a network of parliamentarians around the world organized to promote this kind of initiative. The broad representation of our Canadian group and our international network gives me confidence that there is a high degree of receptivity to and enthusiasm for this initiative, not just by the leaders as we have heard their statements, but also potentially in the Parliaments of the world.
One nation needs to take the lead. It needs to be a nation with an international reputation for support of the United Nations. Canada is in that position. As parliamentarians we owe it to the people of Canada and to the people of the world to press our government to show continued leadership in the creation of an effective United Nations for the 21st century.
So this evening I am asking for colleagues' support, and as I speak in the House and also across Canada for concerned and interested Canadians' public support, in urging the Prime Minister and the Secretary of State for External Affairs to be proactive. When Canada addresses the United Nations General Assembly in New York next Wednesday, I urge Canada's voice to be heard in calling for a UN summit on global security and committing resources to see it come about and lead us to a secure 21st century.

Madam Speaker, colleagues, I thank you for the opportunity to introduce this motion and for your kind attention.

speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I want to start by congratulating the hon. member for Waterloo for this important motion which he has put before Parliament today.
In his motion, as he said, he is asking the Government of Canada to promote a summit meeting at the United Nations on global security and, in particular, to search for ways to prevent aggression by an improved peacekeeping policy and through the enforcement of international law.
Let me acknowledge immediately the outstanding work done so far by the United Nations in peacekeeping since 1956 when we had the first real peacekeeping operation to solve the Suez crisis. Of course, the proposals for that peacekeeping operation were put forward by our foreign minister of the day, Lester B. Pearson, who was, at the time, the President of the General Assembly of the United Nations.
As we all recall, Mr. Pearson won the Nobel Prize for that initiative. There is a long tradition for Canadians taking the kind of initiatives that the hon. member for Waterloo suggests today in his motion.
Over the years, these peacekeeping forces of the United Nations have monitored ceasefire operations. They have supervised elections in countries. They have monitored the withdrawal of armed forces from certain countries. They have also been there to govern the transition of certain colonies to self-government.
In fact as you will recall, UN peacekeeping forces won the Nobel Peace Prize in 1988 for the outstanding work they did over the years in bringing about peace.
All along since 1956, Canada has been one of the great leaders. Since 1948, Canadian peacekeeping forces have participated in 30 countries in peacekeeping operations. Over 80,000 Canadians have been involved in peacekeeping. This year, there are 2,000 of our troops involved but unfortunately again over that time, 81 Canadians were killed in peacekeeping operations.

September 19, 1991
Private Members' Business
As I said, what has been done so far has been good, but we have to admit it is still limited. Improvements are necessary and that is why this summit meeting at the United Nations is essential.
The gulf war in February, the war between Iraq and Kuwait, demonstrated this. The main problem at that time, you will recall, is that the UN peacekeeping forces had to go into operation once Kuwait was occupied by Iraq. It came in after the fact. What we are seeking is a type of UN peacekeeping force and a preventive peacekeeping policy which would have prevented that aggression from taking place in the first place. We are not to act after the fact, after the aggression, but prevent the aggression from taking place.
What we need is a new world order that would provide for preventive peacekeeping. What do we mean by that? We mean a process whereby there would be early warning on potential aggression that would provide for certain peacekeeping. There is no doubt that it is easier and less costly to prevent the occupation of a country such as Kuwait than to evict an aggressor once that occupation has taken place.
How would we set up such a preventive peacekeeping policy, or operation? I might mention that I have a private members' motion before this House which is motion 535 which sets out some of the details for preventive peacekeeping such as I will now discuss before the House.
What we need are, first of all, regionally located standing UN forces made up of national contingents on a rotating basis. When an incident takes place, the Security Council decides that we need a peacekeeping force, and the force is drafted from national contingents at the time.
What I and other experts are suggesting is that UN peacekeeping forces would be stationed on perhaps the six continents of the world in certain friendly countries with contingents made up of many countries. They are trained and they would be trained by special UN training units on how to properly carry out peacekeeping operations, but they would be there ready to respond if a nation felt threatened by the aggression of another country. So, if there was such a threat of aggression, the threatened nation could call upon the Secretary General and the Security Council and there would be a force in that region of the world to immediately go to the border area and patrol the border under the UN flag, the UN
helmets and uniform patches and so on, and with weapons, not heavy weapons, but to deter the aggression.
Now imagine if we had had such a policy before the Kuwait war. If Kuwait, seeing the build-up of forces and the threatening action that was made against it by Iraq, could have called for a regional UN force that would have already been in place in the Middle East somewhere or close by in that part of the world which could go there and station itself along the border between Kuwait and Iraq. It is very unlikely in those circumstances, despite the character of Saddam Hussein, that he would have invaded against a multinational UN force that was already on the border under the UN flag. Not under the United States flag or under the Canadian flag, but under the UN flag. That is what is suggested as a part of a preventive peacekeeping policy.
There would also be, in different parts of the world, probably in the same place as these regional forces, stockpiles of equipment ready to support the forces. Now these forces that would be permanent with national contingents of UN armies or national armies could be supplemented by additional forces from the countries of the world if the thing escalated beyond what was originally considered necessary.
Once the UN force was on the border to deter aggression then you could immediately refer the outstanding issues of the dispute to the Security Council, to the General Assembly, perhaps to the World Court, the International Court of Justice, for mediation, for arbitration to resolve the underlying causes that might lead to that aggression that would have been under way, but which was prevented by the UN force on the spot.
Other things that have to be considered of course are proper financing for such UN operations. Unfortunately, at the United Nations now there is a large sum of arrears for UN peacekeeping operations. I believe it is over $800 million. Most of this, again unfortunately, is owed by the United States and the Soviet Union. That is what I think has to be pursued at greater length at the summit suggested by my hon. friend. As he said, many of these recommendations came out of a forum sponsored by Parliamentarians for Global Action here in Ottawa on May 21 and 22 of this year when 21 parliamentarians from 15 countries, parliamentarians who specialized in these things, came together and discussed this matter with experts for two days and then produced what is
September 19, 1991

called "The Ottawa Declaration on United Nations Collective Security".
I fully support the hon. member's proposal. As I say, there are a lot of good ideas that could be put into more concrete form at such a meeting at the United Nations and all it requires really is the political will. As I say, let us look at the example of Kuwait, how less expensive it would have been in human lives, how less expensive in financial resources if we had had such a preventive peacekeeping policy in force there to prevent the aggression of Iraq. We would not have had to dislodge them from Iraq, we would have prevented the aggression in the first place.

This motion has our support and we would hope that all members of the House will not only support it but restrain their oratory to the point that before six o'clock this bill can receive unanimous approval of this House. I am sure it has that. Those who observe Private Members' Business will know that there is too often a propensity to talk a bill out. If we could have some discipline, perhaps we could put on the record of this House this very important motion, which I am sure reflects the hopes and aspirations of all Canadians.
It is important I think in analysing the motion before us to keep in mind the different concepts of peacekeeping and enforcement that are embodied in the motion which reads:
That, in the opinion of this House, the government promote a summit-level meeting at the United Nations on Global Security, to examine ways of implementing and strengthening the United Nations peacekeeping and enforcement mechanisms.
Canadians are very familiar with the peacekeeping role and potential of the United Nations. We have been involved since the beginning when we were involved in the innovative approach to the UN Charter and the way in which the UN works to get around the rigidities put in the Charter in Articles 43 and 47 to allow the UN itself to play a direct role in keeping the peace. Invariably this role has been confined to coming in after hostilities have
Private Members' Business
broken out to essentially police the peace by putting a UN force between the previously warring parties in the hopes that its presence would deter any future outbreak of hostilities. That is a very important role and one in which Canada has played an important part over the years.
There are important ways in which this role can be strengthened. In passing I note with regret that the government in its defence statement of two days ago included UN peacekeeping only as an afterthought, a paragraph stuck in the statement. It made no commitment to improve the work of the Canadian military in training and preparing itself for a role in peacekeeping.
The government has put a cap on the contributions that Canada will make to peacekeeping, contrary I believe to the will of most Canadians. It is a role that would be very, very effective and important in actually preserving lives and keeping the peace, far less expensive than the waste of money which is reflected in most of the rest of the defence policy of this government. Instead of emphasizing this constructive role, the government is just carrying on.
It is important that we devote much more attention than we have. It is being said privately by generals of other countries that Canada's capacity to contribute in peacekeeping has deteriorated, that we are not doing as good a job as we could.
Our individual soldiers who go overseas do a good professional job, those who are working specifically do a good professional job. However, the collective effort of Canada in this area, the level of training and so forth is not what it should be.
As well, I note we have had a lot of discussion about base closings. The people in the Annapolis Valley have come up with a proposal for long term development of the base in Cornwallis for a number of training purposes, including that of a multinational training centre. It is an idea the government should follow up very quickly and not wait for the report of the advisory committee.
As sort of an extension of peacekeeping, the UN has got into other very important areas, such as the monitoring and verification of elections and the work in Namibia with the police, in which Canada made a contribution.

September 19, 1991
Private Members' Business
The motion goes on to talk about enforcement. This is the area which is going to need an enormous amount of international effort if we are to achieve any significant improvements. The concept behind enforcement is to get involved in a potential military dispute, a potential war, before it breaks out and/or to have sufficient military capacity to enforce the will of the United Nations and the international community where a breach of international law has occurred.
We have had some examples of UN involvement in this way. Neither of the examples reflect an exercise of the UN Charter as it was originally contemplated. The first major one was in Korea where the United Nations Security Council happened to be missing the Soviet Union, which had gone off on a boycott at that stage. The remaining members of the Security Council were able to get together and agree that the response to the North Korean invasion of South Korea would come under UN direction. The command in that case, while it was really American, was officially that of the United Nations. That particular instance has never been duplicated.
In the gulf war, while the Security Council agreed in effect virtually unanimously-and certainly the superpowers, the permanent members of the Security Council all agreed-they were able to get through Security Council resolutions. However, the direction of the forces in the Gulf were not that of the UN but rather that of the member states which decided to contribute to the military response in that case. Therefore, the effect was that the Americans provided the military direction and leadership in concert with the other individual members of the UN who participated. That was not a direct UN operation.
It is probably beyond our hope in the immediate future that a global summit or any other political activity is going to produce such a dramatic change that a military operation the size of the Gulf operation will come under direct UN military supervision. Apart from anything else, the political problems are enormous.
It would be highly unlikely that a government such as the United States, which made such a huge contribution militarily in the Gulf operation, would be prepared in any future operation to turn over the direction of its forces in such a sizeable conflict to the UN or to any other command. However, the UN may be able to move step by step into a far more effective role in less
significant conflicts, in more minor conflicts where the size of the military operation does not have to be as large as in the Gulf where there were 500,000 troops and a major connection between the various forces working together in that particular conflict.
While I support this motion and I support the idea of a global summit, I am inclined to think that the Canadian government should not just leave it at pushing for summits. As we have seen in the case of the arms sales issue, the government's call for a global summit there has evaporated into thin air. It is very hard to get the nations of the world to come together for a global summit unless there is a strong common will. The political effort involved in simply getting them all together, while it is important, should be directed toward more incremental gains and to work at the UN for the development of a UN force that operates in a similar way to the peacekeeping forces where various nations contribute forces to a UN command to work in a specific conflict or dispute. It seems to me that working on that would be a progressive step.
As the member for Waterloo mentioned, I think the UN may also have a role in international surveillance, security communications and development of an exchange of information, in confidence building measures and in other ways to head off disputes.
I recently attended an interesting conference in Windsor on civilian based defence. We heard an interesting address from Gene Sharp, who has written on the subject. There is in fact a civilian based defence association which promotes a series of useful ideas for heading off violent conflict and offering the potential for resolving disputes more effectively without resort to military means.
My final point, if I can, is to relate this motion to the debate that goes on in this House and elsewhere on the future of NATO and the role of NATO and other possible forces in regional conflicts in Europe.
As the cold war is now over and the threat of a Soviet Warsaw Pact invasion into western Europe, if it ever existed, is now gone, what is left in Europe are totally different security questions.
Again, the member for Waterloo mentioned Yugoslavia. That is a totally different security problem from that posed by the Soviet Union and the Warsaw Pact: a
September 19, 1991

massive invasion similar to that in the Second World War.
What is needed to respond there militarily is a small force which can move quickly into that area. The issue then becomes: who runs it? The desirable answer for that is the United Nations. It should have a force which could go into Yugoslavia and deal with it.
Short of the United Nations in the interim, it should be all the nations of Europe including the United States and Canada that have some sort of security arrangement. The least desirable result, in fact non-desirable result, is to have NATO, which was designed for a totally different purpose and has a narrow base of members in the new Europe, taking on the responsibility of being the region's police force.
I urge the House to support this motion. I urge the Canadian people to support the direction of this motion. It is a very important one with great hope for the future of the world.

speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I too wish to lend my support to my hon. colleague's ' motion. It is very important.
The United Nations, as the international community's guardian of peace and security, has obtained a new lease on life from the end of the cold war and a successful outcome of the gulf crisis.
The United Nations can now start to deliver on its promise as the only organization able and mandated by the whole international community to deal with the global issues and challenges.
The Security Council of the United Nations is empowered to recommend and decide on action to be taken to preserve and to maintain international peace and security-
During the cold war it was literally crippled. It was prevented from agreeing on tangible responses to acts of aggression or other threats and defiances. Consequently, the provisions of chapter 7 of the charter of the United Nations was almost never used.
With the end of the east-west confrontation, the world has witnessed a rare degree of co-operation among the council's permanent five and the other non-permanent members of the council.
Private Members' Business
The ability of the Security Council to act in concert is a testimony to the new era of co-operation which is now open to all of us. In fact, the international community was able last year to deal with the severe Iraqi threat to international peace and security in an unprecedented manner, a manner that gave the whole United Nations system a new lease on life.
Iraq's aggression was a litmus test for the United Nations. The successful outcome to that aggression sent a clear message that the world has changed, that it will not tolerate aggression and that international law cannot be ignored.
It is clear that peacekeeping and peacemaking must remain the focus of the council's mandate. Recent events have underlined the promise of peacekeeping. Future trends for peacekeeping operations are to combine traditional military elements with political, humanitarian, economic and sometimes social.
We need those mechanisms. More advanced planning and financing will be needed. However important peacekeeping is, peacemaking must take on a more important role. We all agree that long-term security depends on the development of a more comprehensive apparatus that enables the Security Council to manage not only the crises that have already erupted, but also disputes which threaten to degenerate into crises.
The United Nations' previous inability to bring its members to respect the council's decisions meant that the organization was never able to achieve its potential as a peacemaker. It has never put in place the machinery which would allow the organization itself to enforce peace.
Now that the United Nations has the potential to act in this area, it is important to look at the arrangements that were foreseen in the United Nations charter which could enable the organization to meet its obligations in this regard. These are foreseen in chapter 7 of the charter.
Should we consider activating the provisions of article 43 which ask all members of the United Nations to:
- undertake to make available to the Security Council, on its call and in accordance with a special agreement or arrangements, armed forces, assistance, and facilities, including rights of passage, necessary for the purpose of maintaining international peace and security.

Private Members' Business
Such agreement or arrangements shall govern the numbers and types of forces, their degree of readiness and general location, and the nature of the facilities and assistance to be provided.
Agreement or arrangements shall be negotiated as soon as possible on the initiative of the Security Council. They shall be concluded between the Security Council and members, or between the Security Council and groups of members, and shall be subject to ratification by the signatory states in accordance with their respective constitutional processes.
This is what article 43 of the United Nations charter calls for.
The first request is to make armed forces available to the United Nations. Once this is decided, this route would require the negotiation of agreements specifying the numbers and the types of forces, degree of readiness, the general location, and the nature of facilities and equipment to be provided.
Such an agreement might have the following advantages. The nature of the commitment would be determined in advance, which is very important. Defence authorities would be able to allocate the necessary resources and develop and exercise operational plans. It might be possible to avoid a need to relocate resources on an emergency basis as has often been the case for major Canadian participation in a United Nations peacekeeping mission.
Such an agreement would also allow participation by contributory states in the Security Council's deliberations and decisions concerning the employment of those forces. They would thus have a seat at the table which might not otherwise be available to them.
The events of the past two years have raised the expectations of the people all over the world. The international community now expects stronger council actions and a wide variety and range of conflicts that could jeopardize the international peace and security in a broader sense than was ever envisioned. In these, those events have led to a process of reconsideration of some of the reference points of international relations, including the principle of non-interference in the internal affairs of member states.
In terms of foreign policy, Canadian participation in peacekeeping has always served to reinforce our status as an international player of consequence, and our reliance on multilateralism. I believe that Canadian participation in a renewed concept of international peacemaking
under the United Nations auspices will also serve Canada's image and policies well.
It is my conviction that the United Nations has to change, it has to evolve, so as to be able to execute the mandate given to it by its founders. The strengthening of the United Nations organization and system should become one of our main objectives in the current General Assembly. The strengthening of the United Nations enforcement or peacekeeping mechanisms will be an evolutionary process.

speechtext:
Madam Speaker, it is my pleasure this evening to support the motion before us put by my colleague from Waterloo across the floor. The motion reads:
That, in the opinion of this House, the government promote a summit level meeting at the United Nations on global security, to examine ways of implementing and strengthening the United Nations peacekeeping and enforcement mechanisms.
It is not my intent this evening to talk out this issue because I think it would be an important signal for the Parliament here to approve this motion. I hope that we get an opportunity to do so on this.
When the United Nations was founded at San Francisco on June 25, 1945 its charter was signed by 51 states, primarily the nations of the western hemisphere and Europe. Now, close to half a century later, there are over 160 signatory states, representing all regions and peoples of the globe. The delegates at San Francisco met in the face of a world very different from that facing the delegates today in New York.
Although the original challenges identified at San Francisco, such as economic development, peace and security and human rights remain; many others have risen. The concepts of sustainable development, third world debt, self-determination and high technology were unknown to the framers of the UN Charter. The emergence and persistence of these and many other challenges, coupled with momentous global political change in the last two years, let alone in the last half century, have contributed to a sense of crisis today which did not exist in 1945. There is an increasing demand for a rethinking of the means by which humankind orders its affairs.
The role of the United Nations, the largest multilateral organization in the history of civilization, is both central and critical to this task. As a fundamental supporter of the United Nations system since its inception, Canada's contribution to United Nations reform and an enhanced United Nations presence in world
September 19, 1991

affairs is both necessary and vital to Canada's national interests.
Madam Speaker, I am also, besides being pleased to stand in support of this motion this evening, very pleased to say that I am a member of the organization Parliamentarians For Global Action, an organization which represents a large non-partisan group of parliamentarians from around the globe. As was mentioned by other speakers this evening, representatives of this organization met in Ottawa on May 21 and 22 and produced the Ottawa declaration on UN collective security. Perhaps I can outline just a few of the points that were made in this declaration, which in some respects go a little bit further than the motion before us this evening that we are debating. One of the points made in this declaration is that the rule of law ultimately will prove less costly than the chaos of war.
Earlier this year after the gulf war crisis the Standing Committee on External Affairs and International Trade met on February 6 to hear witnesses from non-government organizations working in Third World countries speak to the problems that the gulf war created for many Third World nations.
It has been suggested that the gulf war, the crisis we have lived through this year and are happy to see the end of, could be only the beginning of north-south wars in our world. Nobody would want to see that happen, but I think it is true that that is a possibility given the amount of militarization and the amount of arms trade that goes on in this world and the frustration that is experienced by so many nations of the south. Unless we are very vigilant and determined that war will not occur again and carry through on such proposals as is presented in the motion this evening, it could be the first of the north-south confrontations in our world.
When the non-government organizations came before our committee and spoke of the cost of the gulf war, not to the developed nations but to the developing Third World southern nations, they spoke of the fact that that war threatened and affected the lives of millions of people in nations all over the world. Who would have imagined that a war that took place in the Middle East would affect countries so disparate in location in our globe as Brazil, Bangladesh, India, Pakistan, Sri Lanka, and the Philippines; but that in fact is what has happened.
Prtivate Members' Business
It is these wars that create more difficult economic circumstances for these already struggling nations, causing standards of living to deteriorate and immediately causing for our own concern large numbers of refugees and insecurity globally speaking.
The declaration that was made in Ottawa spoke of different initiatives that could be taken: preventive peacekeeping where UN troops could be deployed along the border of a nation legitimately fearing attack, to be backed as necessary by forces authorized by the Security Council, as a deterrent to possible aggression by another state and a signal of the resolve of the international community to remain seized of the situation. It requested particular parliamentary initiatives and it stated specifically: "We call upon our colleagues in Parliaments, assemblies, and congresses around the world to begin a major review of the structure of the United Nations with a view to broadening the political legitimacy of the United Nations collective security actions and to ensure that those actions reflect the interests of all member states".
In response to that, the first paragraphs that I read as I stood here in the House this evening were from a notice that was sent out internationally and to colleagues and friends across this country announcing that the Liberal Party of Canada is sponsoring a public symposium entitled "Canada and the United Nations System in the 21st Century", which will take place in Vancouver, British Columbia, beginning on United Nations Day, October 24, and going through to October 26.
At that time we are hoping to discuss the topics of the maintenance of peace, environment and development, trade and development, the movement of peoples, leadership, the UN role in world society, and the role of law.
The very first workshop of that session to which all are invited is entitled "The Maintenance of Peace".
The role of the United Nations in maintaining international peace and security, the powers of the Security Council under chapters 6 and 7 of the charter, residual powers of other organs such as the General Assembly, peacekeeping, the role of the secretary general, options for reform of charter provisions, Security Council membership, and UN versus regional arrangements will all be on the agenda in that workshop.
